title: How Aluwind Got Here
web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: How the Business & Stock Got Here — Past Cycles & Pivots

epigraph.quote: “What began in 2003 as a small fabrication firm in Santacruz, Mumbai, has today grown into one of India’s trusted names in façade and fenestration solutions.”
epigraph.author: Murli Manohar Kabra, Chairman and Managing Director, Annual Report FY2025-26

web_blocks.html: Aluwind was incorporated on 22 April 2003 as Aluwind Architectural Private Limited. Its stated purpose was to take over Alu-Wind Industries, a partnership between Murli Manohar Kabra and Rajesh Kabra [3]. A third brother, Jagmohan Kabra, joined the board in October 2018 and runs manufacturing in Pune; the next generation, Akshat and Govinda Kabra, now serve as Chief Technology Officer and Chief Marketing Officer [1]. Fenestration, the trade word for windows and doors, was the original business. Façades, the glass and aluminium outer skin of a larger building, came later and are now the growth story. The registered office in Malad (West), Mumbai, and the factory land at Koregaon Bhima near Pune are owned; the Pune experience centre in Kalyani Nagar and a Goregaon branch complete the footprint [3].

web_blocks.takeaway: The company has three eras: a slow family-firm era to 2020, an Eternia-led window ramp to 2024, and a façade-led scale-up since 2025 that is straining cash.

web_blocks.html: The early cycle was slow. Revenue from operations was ₹21.28 Cr in FY21, ₹28.99 Cr in FY22 and ₹48.87 Cr in FY23 on the prospectus’s restated basis, while profit after tax stayed under ₹1 Cr in the first two years [3]. The breakout came with Eternia. Projects using Eternia products went from ₹0.57 Cr (2.67% of revenue) in FY21 to ₹25.28 Cr (51.74%) in FY23, and Hindalco supplied 44% of FY23 purchases [3]. That dependence matters because the anchor-partner agreement, signed in December 2023, runs for three years and falls due for renewal in December 2026 [3][4]. I found no public disclosure of renewal terms as of the research cutoff.

web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue grew about 6.5 times from FY21 to FY26, a compound rate near 45% a year, but the margin never held the FY24 peak and cash flow went negative as sales scaled. FY23 PAT is ₹2.74 Cr in the FY26 report; margins for FY21-FY23 exclude other income (restated); H1 FY27 margin is computed from the filing.

web_blocks.html: The FY25 margin dip is the company’s most important past cycle. EBITDA grew just 1.5% (₹11.81 Cr to ₹11.98 Cr) on 31% revenue growth [7]. The margin fell from 14.2% to 11.0%. The filings give no segment margin, so the cause is my inference: larger façade and window contracts, more labour and factory cost (₹15.0 Cr in FY25 and ₹23.3 Cr in FY26) and more rent (₹1.14 Cr to ₹1.87 Cr) as premises were added all arrived before scale benefits did [1]. Profit still rose 7.6% to ₹8.12 Cr, helped by ₹1.30 Cr of other income [7][1]. The back-loaded pattern repeats: H2 FY25 revenue of ₹63.8 Cr was 40% above H1, and receivables kept rising into September 2026 (₹54.7 Cr against ₹39.1 Cr at March), even as inventory fell [7][5].

The IPO was a fixed-price issue of 66,00,000 fresh shares at ₹45, worth ₹29.70 Cr, with no offer for sale. Corpwis Advisors was lead manager and NNM Securities was market maker, holding a reserved 3,30,000 shares [3]. It was subscribed 8.19 times, with 1,796 allottees [23]. Promoters and promoter group fell from 98.22% to 72.13% after the issue and a 62:10 bonus in January 2024 [3][6]. The shareholder register as of September 2026 shows promoters at 72.61% and institutions at 1.17% [6].

The prospectus stated two objects: ₹20.45 Cr for working capital and ₹6.50 Cr for general corporate purposes, with ₹2.75 Cr of estimated issue expenses [3]. The record matches the plan. The statement of deviation for March 2025 shows ₹20.45 Cr used for working capital, ₹6.49 Cr of ₹6.55 Cr for general purposes and ₹2.70 Cr for expenses, with ₹5.67 lakh unused; no monitoring agency was needed [10][11]. An auditor’s certificate dated 10 November 2025 confirms full use, and the FY26 report records no deviation [1]. My judgement: the spending was clean, but a working-capital object cannot be audited for effect. The IPO money was absorbed within a year, because FY25 alone added ₹19.2 Cr of inventory and ₹21.9 Cr of receivables and unbilled work [1].

Compare the promise with the outcome. The prospectus assumed inventory would fall to 72 days of material cost, receivables would run at 114 days and trade payables would be paid in 27 to 29 days, a cycle of about 157 days [3]. The FY26 filed ratios imply inventory of about 167 days, receivables of 90 days and payables of 118 days on the company’s own turnover ratios, a cycle near 139 days [1]. The measures differ in method, so only direction is reliable. Receivables came in better than planned. Inventory is far higher, and suppliers fund the business for about four months, not one. On the Screener basis the cycle is 181 days, worse than the plan (Chapter 3).

Capacity followed the order flow. At the prospectus date the factory covered 45,000 sq ft, with installed capacity of 160,368 m² a year and utilisation of 17%, 24% and 41% in FY21 to FY23 [3]. A second 44,000 sq ft premises was leased in October 2024 [22]. By June 2025 the company stated 18,600 m² a month of capacity at 50% utilisation, and a new CNC (computer-controlled cutting) line added 3,162 m² a month for ₹3.90 Cr including GST, funded by internal accruals and debt [9]. An imported Italian five-axis CNC machine followed, and FY26 plant and machinery additions were ₹4.11 Cr [8][1]. The company also runs an in-house powder-coating line, which applies a durable paint finish to extrusions, and in FY26 it signed a toll agreement so that Eternia’s West and South India window orders can use its idle capacity [2][1].

The latest chapter is about funding. Borrowings rose from ₹13.1 Cr at March 2025 to ₹41.3 Cr at March 2026 and ₹46.1 Cr at September 2026, and the board sought shareholder approval at the 3 September 2026 AGM to raise the borrowing ceiling from ₹125 Cr to ₹200 Cr [1][5]. The order book was ₹302 Cr in May 2025, ₹315 Cr in November 2025 and ₹300 Cr in May 2026, which suggests order inflow roughly matched billing without growing the backlog [7][8][2]. Management guides FY27 revenue to ₹200 Cr. With H1 FY27 at ₹74.0 Cr, the second half must deliver ₹126 Cr, 72% above H2 FY26’s ₹73.1 Cr [2][5]. H2 has exceeded H1 in each year, but never by that margin; I would put the chance of reaching ₹200 Cr at 10% or less.

web_blocks.takeaway: The stock has made one full round trip: from the IPO price to roughly double, and back to the IPO price. Month-end closes are from Yahoo Finance weekly history and can differ slightly from exchange data; the 52-week range of ₹40.0 to ₹85.0 comes from the TradingView snapshot.

web_blocks.html: The share price tells its own version of the cycle. It listed at the issue price, rose to a month-end close of ₹90.9 in October 2025, and by 13 November 2026 had fallen about 51% from that close to ₹44.9, back at the ₹45 IPO price [3][44][43]. The first leg followed order wins and a fast-growing top line. The second leg followed the audited FY26 cash-flow statement, the rise in borrowings and the thin trading in the stock. Chapter 7 returns to what the market is pricing; the point here is that the business cycle and the price cycle moved apart, with profit rising while the shares halved from their peak.

Management turnover also marks this period. The CFO and company secretary both resigned in 2026 and were replaced by Aarti Ahuja and Yashi Gupta [1]. Ajay Porwal, founder of Alphatech Group, joined on 5 November 2026 as President, Global Business and Strategic Alliances to explore exports [5]. The FY26 foreign-exchange outgo of ₹2.78 Cr reflects imports, while foreign-exchange earnings are nil, so the company has no export revenue today [1]. These changes bear on the next chapter, which asks what the company sells and who pays.

book_paragraphs: Let me tell you how I read a company’s past, and then we will do it together for Aluwind. I do not start with the share-sale prospectus or the press release. I start with the question: what did this business look like when nobody was watching? For Aluwind, the answer is a small family fabrication shop in Santacruz, Mumbai, opened in April 2003 when two Kabra brothers took over a partnership called Alu-Wind Industries [3]. A third brother later ran the factory. Their sons now sit in the technology and marketing chairs [1]. It is a family business that learned to work with developers, and it is still run that way.

Two words before we go further. Fenestration is simply windows and doors. A façade is the outer skin of a large building, the glass-and-aluminium wall you see on an office tower. Aluwind began with the first and has been moving, order by order, toward the second.

For seventeen years the company was small. Revenue was ₹21.28 Cr in FY21 and ₹28.99 Cr in FY22, and profit was under ₹1 Cr both years [3]. There were landmarks. About ₹21 Cr of work for Vascon Engineers between 2007 and 2009 [3]. A ₹7 Cr job in Hyderabad in 2013 [3]. A first order from L&T Realty in 2015 that grew into about ₹65 Cr of L&T work by 2022 [3]. But if you had asked an analyst in 2019 to name the company’s edge, the honest answer would have been: relationships and reliability, not scale.

Then came June 2020 and a deal with Eternia, the premium window brand of Hindalco, part of the Aditya Birla Group. Aluwind became an exclusive fabricator, which means it built and installed windows using Eternia’s aluminium sections and design system. Look at what happened next. Eternia projects were ₹0.57 Cr of sales in FY21, 2.67% of the total. By FY23 they were ₹25.28 Cr, 51.74%, and Hindalco supplied 44% of everything Aluwind bought that year [3]. I would call that the company’s first real cycle: a partnership turned a ₹21 Cr firm into a ₹49 Cr firm in two years.

Now ask yourself the question I always ask at this point: what is the catch? The catch is a date. The anchor-partner agreement, which names Aluwind as Eternia’s lead partner in the Mumbai region, was renewed in December 2023 for three years [3][4]. It falls due in December 2026, a few weeks after our research cutoff. I could not find any public record of its renewal terms. That is not a red flag. It is a gap, and I want you to carry it into the chapters ahead.

The listing came next. The company turned public in October 2023, issued bonus shares, and sold 66,00,000 fresh shares at a fixed ₹45 each in a ₹29.70 Cr issue, led by Corpwis Advisors with NNM Securities as market maker [3]. It was subscribed 8.19 times [23]. The promoters went from 98.22% to 72.13% [3][6]. The prospectus said the money would fund ₹20.45 Cr of working capital and ₹6.5 Cr of general corporate needs [3]. I checked the record. The statement filed in May 2025 shows ₹20.45 Cr used for working capital and ₹6.49 Cr for general purposes, with just ₹5.67 lakh left over, and the auditor’s certificate of November 2025 confirms full use [10][1]. So here is a company that spent IPO money as it said it would. Look at the register today: promoters hold 72.61%, institutions 1.17%, and 945 shareholders in all [6]. It is a closely held company with a thin public float.

But there is a second question: did it work? The prospectus assumed inventory would fall to 72 days of material cost, customers would pay in about 114 days and suppliers would be paid in 27 to 29 days, a cycle of about 157 days [3]. The filed ratios for FY26 imply about 167 days of inventory, 90 days of receivables and 118 days of payables, a cycle near 139 days [1]. Customers paid faster than planned. But stock is far higher than planned, and suppliers are funding the business for four months, not one. On the Screener basis the cycle is even longer, 181 days. Chapter 3 explains why.

Let me walk you through the second cycle. FY24 was the peak: revenue ₹83.43 Cr, EBITDA margin about 14.2%, profit ₹7.54 Cr [4][7]. Then FY25 revenue rose 31% to ₹109.22 Cr but EBITDA grew just 1.5% [7]. Think about that for a moment. The company sold 31% more and earned 1.5% more operating profit. The margin dropped from 14.2% to 11.0%. The filings do not give a margin by product, so this is my reading: larger façade jobs, more factory and site labour (₹15.0 Cr in FY25, ₹23.3 Cr in FY26) and more rent all arrived before the scale benefits did [1]. And the cash? Operating cash flow was negative in FY25 and again in FY26, at about ₹18.8 Cr and ₹16.3 Cr [1]. Profit was real, but it went into stock and receivables.

Capacity followed the orders. The factory covered 45,000 sq ft at the time of the prospectus, with utilisation of 17%, 24% and 41% over FY21 to FY23 [3]. (Utilisation here means the share of rated cutting-and-fabrication capacity actually used.) A second 44,000 sq ft building was leased in October 2024 [22]. By June 2025 the company reported 18,600 m² a month at 50% utilisation, and a new computer-controlled cutting line added 3,162 m² a month for ₹3.90 Cr [9]. In FY26 it also signed a toll agreement with Hindalco, which lets Eternia’s West and South India window orders use Aluwind’s idle capacity, and it booked ₹1.57 Cr from that [2][1]. Notice what this says: the company expanded capacity at half utilisation. That is a bet on façade orders.

A name change came in April 2025, from Aluwind Architectural to Aluwind Infra-Tech, with the board citing broader work in infrastructure and technology [1]. A subsidiary for façade cleaning, Aluwind Clean-Tech, was formed a month later. The annual report calls it wholly owned in one place and 60% owned in another; the disclosure table says 60% [1]. It had no revenue in FY26 and lost ₹7.46 lakh, and it lost another ₹8.9 lakh in H1 FY27 [1][5]. It is small enough to ignore financially, and it is a reminder to read the footnotes.

Where does that leave us today? Borrowings went from ₹13.1 Cr to ₹41.3 Cr between March 2025 and March 2026, and to ₹46.1 Cr by September 2026 [1][5]. The order book has hovered around ₹300 Cr for eighteen months: ₹302 Cr in May 2025, ₹315 Cr in November 2025, ₹300 Cr in May 2026 [7][8][2]. Management says FY27 revenue will reach ₹200 Cr. The first half gave ₹74.0 Cr, so the second half must give ₹126 Cr, which is 72% more than the last second half [2][5]. In earlier years the second half beat the first, but never by that much. I would put the chance at 10% or less.

You may be wondering what the share price did while all this was happening. It listed at the ₹45 issue price in April 2024. It climbed to a month-end close of ₹90.9 by October 2025, after a string of L&T and Vascon orders. It has since slid about 51% to ₹44.9, which is where it started. The profit line rose through all of it. The shares fell because the cash-flow statement and the borrowing line told a harder story than the income statement did. We will come back to what that means for the price in Chapter 7 [3][44][43][12][16][1].

One more thing you should know. In 2026 the company lost its CFO and its company secretary and hired replacements, and on 5 November 2026 it appointed Ajay Porwal, founder of the Alphatech Group, to explore exports [1][5]. It has no export revenue today. Change at the top is not bad news in itself, but a company that is growing fast on borrowed working capital needs steady hands in finance. We will see how that plays out. First, though, we need to understand what Aluwind actually sells, which is where we go next.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Aluwind’s history is a story of three cycles, and each one began with a partner and ended with a cash question. The Eternia tie-up lifted sales; the façade push lifted order size; the cost of both was paid in inventory and unpaid bills. When you read the next chapters, keep one test in mind: does each rupee of new revenue arrive with a rupee of new cash, or with a bank loan?
